justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I inferred was a starting price around 503–505, with the 1-day estimate of 506 essentially anchored to near-term momentum and mean-reversion tendencies in equity or asset prices. The 1-week estimate of 508 incorporates a slight continuation of that drift, acknowledging that short-term trends tend to persist weakly but not dramatically. The 1-month estimate of 515 extrapolates a gentle upward bias consistent with a long-run positive drift assumption, similar to what one might apply using a simple random walk with drift calibrated to historical returns. None of these estimates assume a major directional catalyst; they are largely driven by statistical baseline expectations rather than any specific fundamental view.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds over time. At the 1-day horizon, the relatively tight interval of 492–520 reflects the fact that daily volatility in most liquid assets is bounded in the short run, absent a shock. By one week, the interval widens to 482–535, capturing the accumulation of several days of potential variance. At one month, the interval of 460–570 is substantially wider, reflecting roughly four weeks of compounding uncertainty. The width scaling is broadly consistent with a square-root-of-time volatility expansion, though I applied some additional uncertainty at longer horizons to account for regime shifts and fat-tailed return distributions that a simple Gaussian model would understate.

There are meaningful tail risks that could push outcomes outside even my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden macro shock — such as an unexpected central bank policy shift, a geopolitical escalation, or a credit event — could easily produce moves well below 492 even within a single day. Liquidity crises or flash crashes represent another source of extreme downside that is structurally underweighted in normal volatility estimates. On the upside, a strong positive surprise such as an unexpectedly favorable economic data release, a policy reversal, or a major short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above 520 in a single session.

Over the one-month horizon, the risks compound further. Structural changes in market sentiment, shifts in interest rate expectations, or sector-specific developments could all generate outcomes that lie entirely outside the 460–570 range. I would emphasize that my stated 90% confidence intervals carry real epistemic uncertainty of their own — the true coverage probability depends heavily on distributional assumptions that are themselves uncertain. Outcomes outside the stated range should not be considered implausible; they simply reflect the less probable portion of the distribution as I modeled it.
